DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
The pilot data in this study is good, but the analysis contradicts it. Table 1 shows that flats participate at a third of the rate of houses, and that overall participation was 57%. The text then calls participation "broadly similar" and projects tonnage using **64%**. Once the projection is corrected, the disposal saving falls and the funding cushion disappears. The projected tonnage is also well above the capacity Brookfield has offered, which the study doesn't address. On the current evidence, the claims that the service is "uniform" and "fully funded" are not supported.

## 1. Participation in flats was very different from houses

Table 1 shows:
- **Houses: 66%** participation, 1.9 kg per participating household per week
- **Flats: 21%** participation, 1.4 kg

That is a threefold difference, and the yield per participating flat is also lower. The study's statement that participation was "broadly similar across housing types", and its recommendation of a uniform service with no separate approach for flats, both contradict its own data. Flats usually need a different approach, such as communal bins, different collection points or targeted engagement. About 10,400 households in the district are flats.

## 2. The projection uses 64%, but the pilot shows 57%

Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate". Table 1 gives **57%** overall, and 64% doesn't appear anywhere in the pilot data. Recalculating with the pilot's own figures by housing type (flats are 20% of households in both the pilot and the district):

| | Households | Participation | kg per week | Tonnes per year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ~2,713 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ~159 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **~2,870** |

That is about **2,870 tonnes, not 3,290**, roughly 13% lower. The "All" row's 1.9 kg is also rounded up from a weighted average of 1.86 kg.

## 3. Brookfield can't take this much

Brookfield has offered **up to 1,800 tonnes a year** until 2029. Even the corrected projection of about 2,870 tonnes leaves around **1,070 tonnes a year** with no contracted treatment. On the study's own 3,290-tonne figure, the gap is nearly 1,500 tonnes. The surplus would have to:

- go to the plant **46 miles away**, with longer journeys, more vehicle and crew time, and a gate fee that isn't stated; or
- stay in the residual waste and be incinerated, which reduces the saving.

The author's description that "treatment is local" only holds for about 60% of the food waste. The study doesn't cost the alternatives.

## 4. The council's net cost exceeds the funding

With the corrected tonnage:

- Disposal saving: about 2,870 × £74 ≈ **£212,000**, not £243,000
- Net cost: £733,400 − £212,000 ≈ **£521,000**
- Provisional new-burdens allocation: **£520,000**

So before any extra haulage or gate fees for the surplus tonnage, the service already **slightly exceeds** the funding. The "about £30,000 headroom" in the original figures relies on the incorrect 64% figure. The allocation is also only **provisional**, and section 5 says only that the Government has "indicated" funding will be provided.

## 5. Gaps in the cost table

The arithmetic in Table 2 is correct:

- Vehicles: £990,000 ÷ 7 ≈ £141,400
- Crews: 12 × £34,000 = £408,000
- Total: £733,400

But some costs seem to be missing:

- **Crew on-costs and cover.** £34,000 may be salary only. Employer's National Insurance, pension contributions, and cover for leave and sickness can add 25–35%.
- **A spare vehicle.** Six vehicles for six crews leaves nothing for breakdowns or servicing.
- **Capital financing.** Depreciation is included, but not interest or borrowing costs.
- **Haulage to the 46-mile plant** for the surplus tonnage.
- **Liners after the first three months.** It isn't clear whether the council will keep supplying them.

## 6. The pilot may overstate long-term performance

- **Six months, January to June.** This misses summer and the late-autumn seasons, and the results may include a novelty effect.
- **The 81% satisfaction figure** comes from "surveyed pilot households". The response rate and the share of non-participants who responded aren't given. Satisfied participants are more likely to answer a survey.

## 7. The timetable has no contingency

Vehicles must be ordered by December for delivery in March. Collections start in early April. All 52,000 caddies are delivered in March, and crews are recruited in February. A delay of a few weeks in any one of these would push back the start date. The study should say what happens if vehicles arrive late, for example a phased roll-out by area.

## What holds up

- The participation rates for each row of Table 1 are calculated correctly.
- The cost table's arithmetic is correct.
- The £74-per-tonne saving per diverted tonne is correct.
- Measuring participation weekly by housing type is good practice. That data is exactly what exposes the problem with flats.
- Low contamination and falling missed-collection reports are encouraging.

## Suggested revisions

1. **Correct the projection** to the pilot's 57% overall rate, or calculate it by housing type, giving about 2,870 tonnes. Restate the disposal saving and the net cost.
2. **Remove the "broadly similar" claim** and propose a specific approach for flats, with its own cost.
3. **Set out a treatment plan for the tonnage above 1,800 tonnes**, with gate fees and haulage costs for the 46-mile plant, or another option.
4. **Show the funding position realistically**: net cost against the provisional allocation, with a sensitivity range and the risk if the allocation turns out lower.
5. **Add the missing costs**: crew on-costs and cover, a spare vehicle, financing, and ongoing liners.
6. **Add contingency to the timetable**, such as a phased start if vehicles are late.

The service is a legal requirement, so the question for Cabinet isn't whether to roll it out. But Cabinet should approve it knowing it is likely to need council funding beyond the new-burdens allocation, and that treatment capacity is still unresolved. The study currently presents it as fully funded, with local treatment in place.
